# BAckground and justification 

novel cross-sectional claim count models for vehicle insurance built upon the combinedd actuarial neural network (CANN) framework proposed by Wüthrich and Merz. The CANN approach combines a classical actuarial model, such as a generalized linear model, with a neural network. This blending of models results in a two-component model comprising a classical regression model and a neural network part. 

The CANN model leverages the strengths of both components, providing a solid foundation and interpretability from the classical model while harnessing the flexibility and capacity to capture intricate relationships and interactions offered by the neural network. In our proposed models, we use well-known log-linear claim count regression models for the classical regression part and a multilayer perceptron (MLP) for the neural network part. The MLP part is used to process telematics car driving data given as a vector characterizing the driving behavior of each insured driver. 

Reproduction of the cross-sectional models of Duval, Boucher & Pigeon (2024), fit on
the public So, Boucher & Valdez (2021) synthetic telematics portfolio.
The objectif is to compare and constrast the predictive and interpretatbility of 
- a glm model 
- a glm model + a neural network layer to model the non ,linearity of telematrics

freq_table <- function(data, var){

  data %>%
    group_by(.data[[var]]) %>%
    summarise(
      Exposure = sum(Exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
      Claims = sum(NB_Claim, na.rm = TRUE),
      Frequency = Claims / Exposure,
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(all_of(var), Frequency, Exposure)
}

Looking at the exposure and frequency graph  by variable(age , sex ,carAge, Credit scoreYears no claims  )

```{r expo_freq plot function}

plot_freq_expo <- function(data, var, var_categorical) {
  
  summary_df <- data %>%
    group_by(.data[[var]], .data[[var_categorical]]) %>%
    summarise(
      Exposure = sum(Exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
      Claims = sum(NB_Claim, na.rm = TRUE),
      Frequency = Claims / Exposure,
      .groups = "drop"
    )
  
  max_expo <- max(summary_df$Exposure, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  ggplot(summary_df,
         aes(x = .data[[var]],
             colour = .data[[var_categorical]],
             fill = .data[[var_categorical]])) +
    
    geom_col(
      aes(y = Exposure),position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_line(
      aes(y = Frequency * max_expo,group = .data[[var_categorical]] ),linewidth = 1.2) +
    
    scale_y_continuous(
      name = "Exposure",
      sec.axis = sec_axis(
        ~ . / max_expo,name = "Frequency")
    ) +
    
    labs(title = paste("Exposure and Frequency by", var),
      x = var,colour = var_categorical,fill = var_categorical) +
    theme_minimal()
}
```

## 5. Modeling 

we will build and compare two models : 
- A glm build and optimised only on the classical variables 
- A hybrid MLP that is initialized at glm coeffciients for traditional variables and find 
non linear relations on telematic variables 

### 5.1 GLM : POIsson vs Negative Binomial

if the variance is quite superior to the mean then we have overdisperssion and
NB distribution is more appropriate 
```{r}
mean(dt2$NB_Claim)
var(dt2$NB_Claim)
dispersion <- var(dt2$NB_Claim) / mean(dt2$NB_Claim)

dispersion
```
very low overdispersion so Poisson might be more appropriate 

```{r poisson_vs_nb}
# Parameters estimated from the data
lambda <- mean(dt2$NB_Claim)

fit_nb <- fitdistr(dt2$NB_Claim, "Negative Binomial")

size <- fit_nb$estimate["size"]
mu   <- fit_nb$estimate["mu"]

obs <- sort(dt2$NB_Claim)

n <- length(obs)
# theorical poisson quantiles 
theo_pois <- qpois(
  ppoints(n),
  lambda = lambda
)
#theorical NB quantiles 
theo_nb <- qnbinom(
  ppoints(n),
  size = size,
  mu = mu
)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

qqplot(theo_pois, obs,
        main = "Poisson QQ Plot",
  xlab = "Theoretical Poisson quantiles",
  ylab = "Observed claim-count quantiles",
       pch = 19, col = "blue")
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)

qqplot(theo_nb, obs,
       main = "Negative Binomial",
  xlab = "Theoretical Negative Binomial quantiles",
  ylab = "Observed claim-count quantiles",
       pch = 19, col = "darkgreen")
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

by comparing the distribution of nb_claims , we clearly see that negative binomial distribution 
is a far better fit for our data 

we will now compare AIC directly (what is AIC ?) 
```{r poisson_vsnb_aic}
pois_fit <- glm(
  NB_Claim ~ 1,
  family = poisson,
  data = dt2
)

nb_fit <- MASS::glm.nb(
  NB_Claim ~ 1,
  data = dt2
)

AIC(pois_fit, nb_fit)
```
The Akaike Information Criterion balances:

- model fit, through the likelihood;
- model complexity, through a penalty for the number of parameters.

**AIC=2k−2log(L)**

where k is the number of estimated parameters and L is the maximized likelihood.

Both distributions have very close AIC ,ans as expected the NB has a slighty lower AIC
so we will choose to model using a Negative binomial distribution. 

### 5.2 Split the dataset into trainig and testing 
```{r split}
# new column that tells us if there is a claim or not 
dt2$HasClaim =as.integer(dt2$NB_Claim > 0)

stratified_split <- function(n_idx, strata, p_train = 0.8, seed = 123) {
  set.seed(seed)
  parts <- lapply(split(n_idx, strata), function(idx) {
    idx <- sample(idx); n <- length(idx)
    n_tr <- floor(p_train * n)
    list(train = idx[seq_len(n_tr)],
         
         test  = idx[-seq_len(n_tr)])
  })
  list(train = unlist(lapply(parts, `[[`, "train"), use.names = FALSE),
       test  = unlist(lapply(parts, `[[`, "test"),  use.names = FALSE))
}
sp <- stratified_split(
seq_len(nrow(dt2)),
dt2$HasClaim,
p_train = 0.8
)
train_dt <- dt2[sp$train,]
test_dt <- dt2[sp$test,]

cat("rows:", nrow(train_dt), nrow(test_dt), "\n")
cat(
"claim rate by split:",
mean(train_dt$HasClaim),
mean(test_dt$HasClaim), "\n"
)
```

first we will construct two models 
```{r}
mod_poi <- glm(
NB_Claim ~ 1,
family = poisson(),
offset = log(Exposure),
data = train_dt
)

mod_nb <- MASS::glm.nb(
NB_Claim ~ offset(log(Exposure)),
data = train_dt
)
```

# 6. Predicting using both stepwise and full variables models 


```{r predicting all bvariables vs stepwise vars}
# Full negative-binomial model predictions
test_dt$pred_nb_full <- predict(
  all_vars_nb,
  newdata = test_dt,
  type = "response"
)

# Stepwise negative-binomial model predictions
test_dt$pred_nb_step <- predict(
  stepwise_nb,
  newdata = test_dt,
  type = "response"
)
#Compare observed and predicted portfolio frequencies
total_exposure <- sum(test_dt$Exposure,na.rm = TRUE)
obs_freq <- sum(test_dt$NB_Claim,na.rm = TRUE) / total_exposure

pred_freq_full <- sum(test_dt$pred_nb_full,na.rm = TRUE) / total_exposure
pred_freq_step <- sum(test_dt$pred_nb_step,na.rm = TRUE) / total_exposure

frequency_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c(
    "Observed",
    "Full NB",
    "Stepwise NB"
  ),
  Frequency = c(
    obs_freq,
    pred_freq_full,
    pred_freq_step
  )
)

# calibration errors 
frequency_comparison$Difference_from_observed <- c(
  0,
  pred_freq_full - obs_freq,
  pred_freq_step - obs_freq
)

frequency_comparison$Relative_difference_pct <- c(
  0,
  100 * (pred_freq_full - obs_freq) / obs_freq,
  100 * (pred_freq_step - obs_freq) / obs_freq
)

frequency_comparison

```

# 7. Diagnostic des erreurs des deux modèles

Given that we're predicting claim counts (NB_Claim) with an exposure offset, we will
compare (explain each metrics using math formulas ) :

- MAE # erreur aboslute moyenne
- RMSE # erreur quadratique moyenne 
- Log-loss binomiale négative : Une valeur plus faible indique un meilleur modèle probabiliste.
- Distribution of residuals
- Observed vs Predicted frequencies

**1.Errors metrics calculations**
a function to calculate the errors metrics, given the predicted y and the observed yis

```{r calculate_errors_metrics}

eval_nb_metrics <- function(y, pred, theta) {

  # Keep only valid observations
  valid <- is.finite(y) &
    is.finite(pred) &
    pred > 0 &
    y >= 0

  y_valid <- y[valid]
  pred_valid <- pred[valid]

  if (length(y_valid) == 0L) {
    stop("No valid observations available.")
  }

  if (!is.finite(theta) || theta <= 0) {
    stop("Theta must be finite and strictly positive.")
  }

  # Individual negative-binomial log-loss
  individual_nb_logloss <- -dnbinom(
    x = y_valid,
    mu = pred_valid,
    size = theta,
    log = TRUE
  )

  # Standard error metrics
  residuals <- y_valid - pred_valid

  mae <- mean(abs(residuals))

  rmse <- sqrt(
    mean(residuals^2)
  )

  # Total and mean negative-binomial log-loss
  total_nb_logloss <- sum(individual_nb_logloss)
  mean_nb_logloss <- mean(individual_nb_logloss)

  data.frame(
    N = length(y_valid),
    Theta = theta,
    MAE = mae,
    RMSE = rmse,
    Total_NB_LogLoss = total_nb_logloss,
    Mean_NB_LogLoss = mean_nb_logloss
  )
}

metrics_full_nb <- eval_nb_metrics(
  y = test_dt$NB_Claim,
  pred = test_dt$pred_nb_full,
  theta = all_vars_nb$theta
)

metrics_step_nb <- eval_nb_metrics(
  y = test_dt$NB_Claim,
  pred = test_dt$pred_nb_step,
  theta = stepwise_nb$theta
)

nb_metrics_comparison <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  `Full NB` = metrics_full_nb,
  `Stepwise NB` = metrics_step_nb,
  .id = "Model"
)

nb_metrics_comparison

```

stepwise model minimises the nb log loss, in fact it has lower value in all errors metrics
as compared to the full variables model 

# 7.1 comparing individual errors NB 
Chaque police reçoit une contribution individuelle à la log-loss : Une valeur élevée signifie que le résultat observé était peu probable selon le modèle.
```{r indivisual errors comparison }
comp_df <- test_dt %>%
  transmute(
    NB_Claim,
    Exposure,

    # Predicted claim counts
    pred_full = pred_nb_full,
    pred_step = pred_nb_step,

    # Raw residuals
    resid_full = NB_Claim - pred_nb_full,
    resid_step = NB_Claim - pred_nb_step,

    # Absolute individual errors
    abs_error_full = abs(NB_Claim - pred_nb_full),
    abs_error_step = abs(NB_Claim - pred_nb_step),

    # Squared individual errors
    squared_error_full =
      (NB_Claim - pred_nb_full)^2,

    squared_error_step =
      (NB_Claim - pred_nb_step)^2,

    # Individual negative-binomial log-loss
    nb_logloss_full = -dnbinom(
      NB_Claim,
      mu = pred_nb_full,
      size = all_vars_nb$theta,
      log = TRUE
    ),

    nb_logloss_step = -dnbinom(
      NB_Claim,
      mu = pred_nb_step,
      size = stepwise_nb$theta,
      log = TRUE
    )
  )
```

Déterminer le meilleur modèle pour chaque police
```{r}
comp_df <- comp_df %>%
  mutate(
    better_model_nb = case_when(
      nb_logloss_full < nb_logloss_step ~ "Full NB",
      nb_logloss_step < nb_logloss_full ~ "Stepwise NB",
      TRUE ~ "Tie"
    )
  )

# compter le modele qui a le plsu de victoire 
individual_nb_wins <- comp_df %>%
  count(better_model_nb) %>%
  mutate(
    percentage = 100 * n / sum(n)
  )

individual_nb_wins
```
stepwise is far better 
Pour chaque police :

- la plus petite log-loss individuelle correspond au modèle qui attribuait la plus grande probabilité au résultat réellement observé ;

- une égalité signifie que les deux modèles attribuaient pratiquement la même probabilité.

plot_age_fit_plotly <- function(data, model) {

  # Check required columns
  required_cols <- c(
    "Insured.age",
    "Exposure",
    "NB_Claim"
  )

  missing_cols <- setdiff(
    required_cols,
    names(data)
  )

  if (length(missing_cols) > 0L) {
    stop(
      "Missing columns: ",
      paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }

  # Check exposure
  if (any(
    !is.finite(data$Exposure) |
      data$Exposure <= 0
  )) {
    stop("Exposure must be finite and strictly positive.")
  }

  # Work on a copy to avoid modifying the original data
  plot_data <- data

  # Predicted claim counts from the stepwise model
  plot_data$pred <- predict(
    model,
    newdata = plot_data,
    type = "response"
  )

  # Aggregate observed and predicted claims by age
  age_df <- plot_data %>%
    filter(
      !is.na(Insured.age),
      is.finite(pred)
    ) %>%
    group_by(Insured.age) %>%
    summarise(
      Exposure = sum(
        Exposure,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

      Claims_obs = sum(
        NB_Claim,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

      Claims_pred = sum(
        pred,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),

      Obs_Freq = if_else(
        Exposure > 0,
        Claims_obs / Exposure,
        NA_real_
      ),

      Pred_Freq = if_else(
        Exposure > 0,
        Claims_pred / Exposure,
        NA_real_
      ),

      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    arrange(Insured.age)

  # Plot
  plot_ly() %>%

    # Exposure bars
    add_bars(
      data = age_df,
      x = ~Insured.age,
      y = ~Exposure,
      name = "Exposure",
      marker = list(
        color = "skyblue"
      ),
      opacity = 0.6,
      yaxis = "y",
      hovertemplate = paste(
        "Age: %{x}",
        "<br>Exposure: %{y:.2f}",
        "<extra></extra>"
      )
    ) %>%

    # Observed frequency line
    add_lines(
      data = age_df,
      x = ~Insured.age,
      y = ~Obs_Freq,
      name = "Observed frequency",
      line = list(
        color = "red",
        width = 3
      ),
      yaxis = "y2",
      hovertemplate = paste(
        "Age: %{x}",
        "<br>Observed frequency: %{y:.4f}",
        "<extra></extra>"
      )
    ) %>%

    # Observed frequency markers
    add_markers(
      data = age_df,
      x = ~Insured.age,
      y = ~Obs_Freq,
      name = "Observed frequency",
      marker = list(
        color = "red",
        size = 6
      ),
      yaxis = "y2",
      showlegend = FALSE,
      hovertemplate = paste(
        "Age: %{x}",
        "<br>Observed frequency: %{y:.4f}",
        "<br>Observed claims: %{customdata}",
        "<extra></extra>"
      ),
      customdata = ~Claims_obs
    ) %>%

    # Stepwise predicted frequency line
    add_lines(
      data = age_df,
      x = ~Insured.age,
      y = ~Pred_Freq,
      name = "Stepwise predicted frequency",
      line = list(
        color = "darkgreen",
        width = 3,
        dash = "dash"
      ),
      yaxis = "y2",
      hovertemplate = paste(
        "Age: %{x}",
        "<br>Predicted frequency: %{y:.4f}",
        "<extra></extra>"
      )
    ) %>%

    # Stepwise predicted frequency markers
    add_markers(
      data = age_df,
      x = ~Insured.age,
      y = ~Pred_Freq,
      name = "Stepwise predicted frequency",
      marker = list(
        color = "darkgreen",
        size = 5,
        symbol = "diamond"
      ),
      yaxis = "y2",
      showlegend = FALSE,
      hovertemplate = paste(
        "Age: %{x}",
        "<br>Predicted frequency: %{y:.4f}",
        "<br>Predicted claims: %{customdata:.2f}",
        "<extra></extra>"
      ),
      customdata = ~Claims_pred
    ) %>%

    layout(
      title = list(
        text = paste(
          "Observed vs Stepwise Predicted Frequency",
          "by Insured Age"
        )
      ),

      xaxis = list(
        title = "Insured age"
      ),

      # Main left axis for exposure

      ),

        t = 100,
        r = 80
      )
    )
}

############en dof fisrt step ###############"""

# 8. CANN model 
here we build a neural network that will be initialsed with the glm and trained to 
understand the hiden non linear relationship hidden in the telematrics datasets 
The CANN blends a classical regression with a network by adding their linear predictors before the link: 

```
log( mu_i ) = log(exposure_i)                    <- offset
            + x_i^trad . beta                    <- log-linear (actuarial) part
            + MLP( x_i^trad , x_i^tele )         <- network (boosting) part
```
Two design decisions carry the whole idea and must not be skipped:
- The log-linear part receives ONLY traditional risk factors. It is deliberately constrained — it provides the stable, interpretable backbone.
- The MLP receives traditional AND telematics inputs, so it can learn interactions BETWEEN them, not just telematics effects in isolation. This is exactly what the paper argues a manually engineered feature set cannot do.

**Warm start**: β is initialised at GLM-A's fitted coefficients, and the MLP's output
layer is initialised at zero. At epoch 0 the CANN is numerically identical to GLM-A;
gradient descent can only move away from it in directions that improve the
likelihood.

## 8.1 Preparation des variables 
```{r}

# VARIABLES
trad_numeric <- c("Insured.age", "Car.age", "Credit.score", "Years.noclaims", "Annual.miles.drive")
trad_factors <- c("Insured.sex", "Marital", "Region", "Car.use.grp")

telematics_selected <- c(
  "Pct.drive.thr",
  "Pct.drive.rush.pm",
  "Accel.06miles",
  "Brake.06miles",
  "Left.turn.intensity08",
  "Right.turn.intensity10"
)

###################################################
# ALIGN FACTOR LEVELS
###################################################

for(v in trad_factors){

  train_dt[[v]] <- factor(train_dt[[v]])

  test_dt[[v]] <- factor(
    test_dt[[v]],
    levels = levels(train_dt[[v]])
  )
}

###################################################
# STANDARDIZATION PARAMETERS
###################################################

std_from_train <- function(x){

  list(
    mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd   = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

}

trad_stats <- lapply(
  train_dt[, ..trad_numeric],
  std_from_train
)

tele_stats <- lapply(
  train_dt[, ..telematics_selected],
  std_from_train
)

###################################################
# SCALING FUNCTION
###################################################

scale_block <- function(data, vars, stats){

  m <- sapply(vars, function(v){

    (data[[v]] - stats[[v]]$mean) /
      stats[[v]]$sd

  })

  m <- as.matrix(m)

  colnames(m) <- vars

  m
}

###################################################
# BRANCH 1 : GLM/TRADITIONAL VARIABLES
###################################################

f_trad <- ~

  Insured.sex +
  Marital +
  Region +
  Car.use.grp +

  Insured.age +
  Car.age +
  Years.noclaims +
  Credit.score

X_trad_train <- model.matrix(
  f_trad,
  data = train_dt
)

X_trad_test <- model.matrix(
  f_trad,
  data = test_dt
)

###################################################
# BRANCH 2 : TELEMATICS VARIABLES
###################################################

X_tele_train <- scale_block(
  train_dt,
  telematics_selected,
  tele_stats
)

X_tele_test <- scale_block(
  test_dt,
  telematics_selected,
  tele_stats
)

###################################################
# TARGET
###################################################

y_train <- train_dt$NB_Claim
y_test  <- test_dt$NB_Claim

###################################################
# OFFSET
###################################################

offset_train <- log(train_dt$Exposure)
offset_test  <- log(test_dt$Exposure)

###################################################
# GLM COEFFICIENTS FOR WARM START
###################################################

beta_glm <- coef(mod_full_nb)

###################################################
# CHECKS
###################################################

cat(
  "X_trad_train:",
  dim(X_trad_train),
  "\n"
)

cat(
  "X_tele_train:",
  dim(X_tele_train),
  "\n"
)

cat(
  "Length y_train:",
  length(y_train),
  "\n"
)

cat(
  "Length beta_glm:",
  length(beta_glm),
  "\n"
)

###################################################
# VERIFY DESIGN MATRIX VS GLM
###################################################

names(beta_glm)

colnames(X_trad_train)
```
